title: Digital Money and Tokenisation for Firms
summary: A ten-module programme helping banks, payment firms, asset managers and infrastructures decide whether and how to participate in digital money and tokenisation.
intro: This training programme equips banks, payment firms, asset managers and market infrastructures to decide whether and how to participate in stablecoins, tokenised deposits, CBDCs and tokenised securities and funds, and to manage the risks.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give strategy, product, risk, compliance, treasury and operations staff a clear, vendor-neutral understanding of the new forms of digital money and tokenised assets and how they are reshaping payments, settlement and asset management. Participants leave able to test the business case, identify the legal, prudential, operational and financial crime risks, and design the governance and controls a supervisor would expect before the firm commits.
sections.What It Covers: The forms of digital money and the singleness of money, stablecoin design and reserves, tokenised deposits, central bank digital currencies, tokenised securities and funds, settlement and market infrastructure, legal certainty and custody, prudential and accounting treatment, financial crime and operational resilience, and building the firm's participation strategy.
Intended Audience: Strategy, product, treasury and payments staff at banks, payment and e-money firms evaluating digital money
Asset managers, custodians, fund administrators and market infrastructure staff working on tokenisation
Compliance, risk, legal and finance professionals who must assess and control new digital money and tokenisation initiatives
Learning Objectives: Explain the main forms of digital money and tokenised assets and how they differ in claim, issuer and risk
Evaluate the business case for issuing, distributing, holding or settling in digital money and tokenised assets
Assess the legal, prudential, accounting and operational risks of participation
Apply financial crime, custody and resilience controls to digital money and tokenised products
Identify the international standards and supervisory expectations relevant to the firm's plans
Design a participation strategy and governance framework the firm can evidence to supervisors
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Modules combine briefings with case studies, decision frameworks and group exercises, and can be selected or tailored to banks, payment firms, asset managers or market infrastructures.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of payments, banking, asset management or market infrastructure is helpful. No technical background in blockchain is required.
Core Reading: BIS, Annual Economic Report 2023, Chapter III: Blueprint for the Future Monetary System
FSB, High-level Recommendations for the Regulation, Supervision and Oversight of Global Stablecoin Arrangements (2023)
FSB, The Financial Stability Implications of Tokenisation (2024)
Basel Committee, Prudential Treatment of Cryptoasset Exposures (2022)

modules.title: The Changing Nature of Money and Settlement
modules.summary: How central bank money, commercial bank money and new private digital money relate to each other, and why programmable ledgers are prompting firms to rethink payments and settlement.
objectives: Distinguish the forms of money by issuer, claim and protection
Explain the singleness of money and why it matters to firms
Identify where tokenisation changes payments and settlement economics
syllabus: Central bank, commercial bank and private digital money
Singleness of money, convertibility at par and confidence
Shared ledgers, programmability and atomic settlement
The BIS and CPMI vision of a tokenised unified ledger

modules.title: Stablecoins: Design, Reserves and Use Cases
modules.summary: How stablecoins are structured and used, what determines whether they hold their value, and the questions a firm should ask before issuing, distributing, holding or accepting them.
objectives: Classify stablecoin designs and stabilisation mechanisms
Evaluate reserve quality, redemption rights and run risk
Assess use cases in payments, trading and cross-border settlement
syllabus: Single-currency, multi-asset and algorithmic designs
Reserve composition, custody, attestation and redemption
De-pegging episodes and lessons for firms
FSB recommendations on global stablecoin arrangements

modules.title: Tokenised Deposits and Bank-Issued Digital Money
modules.summary: How banks can represent deposits on a ledger, how tokenised deposits differ from stablecoins, and the strategic, prudential and interoperability choices facing banks and their corporate clients.
objectives: Explain how tokenised deposits work and how they differ from stablecoins
Evaluate use cases in treasury, trade finance and wholesale settlement
Assess the prudential, deposit protection and interoperability implications
syllabus: Tokenised deposits versus stablecoins: claim, regulation and protection
Programmable payments, corporate treasury and intraday liquidity
Interbank interoperability and settlement in central bank money
Basel Committee treatment of tokenised traditional assets

modules.title: Central Bank Digital Currencies
modules.summary: The design choices behind retail and wholesale CBDCs, the role central banks expect intermediaries to play, and what CBDC adoption could mean for deposits, payments revenue and operations.
objectives: Distinguish retail and wholesale CBDC models and their design choices
Identify the roles intermediaries may play in distribution and services
Assess the impact on the firm's deposits, liquidity and payments business
syllabus: Retail and wholesale CBDCs: purpose, architecture and privacy
Two-tier models, holding limits and intermediary obligations
Deposit disintermediation and liquidity implications
Cross-border CBDC projects and multi-currency platforms

modules.title: Tokenised Securities and Funds
modules.summary: How bonds, equities, money market and other funds are tokenised, issued and distributed, and what tokenisation changes for asset managers, distributors, transfer agents and investors.
objectives: Explain how securities and fund units are tokenised and issued
Evaluate the business case for asset managers and distributors
Identify investor protection and product governance issues
syllabus: Native digital issuance versus tokenised representations
Tokenised funds: registers, transfer agency and distribution
Tokenised money market funds as collateral and cash management
Disclosure, suitability and product governance for tokenised products

modules.title: Market Infrastructure, Settlement and Interoperability
modules.summary: How tokenised trading, clearing and settlement work, how they interact with existing infrastructure, and the settlement finality and interoperability questions market infrastructures and their users must resolve.
objectives: Explain on-chain trading, clearing and delivery versus payment
Assess settlement finality, cash leg and collateral mobility issues
Evaluate interoperability between tokenised and traditional infrastructure
syllabus: Delivery versus payment and atomic settlement on shared ledgers
The cash leg: central bank money, tokenised deposits or stablecoins
PFMI principles applied to tokenised arrangements
Bridges, messaging standards and fragmentation risk

modules.title: Legal Certainty, Custody and Smart Contracts
modules.summary: The legal foundations that make digital money and tokenised assets work, including the nature of the holder's claim, custody and insolvency protection, and the enforceability of smart contracts.
objectives: Assess the legal nature of tokens and the holder's rights
Evaluate custody models and insolvency protection for tokenised assets
Identify smart contract and governance risks requiring legal and technical control
syllabus: Legal characterisation of tokens and linkage to the underlying asset
Custody, segregation and protection in insolvency
Smart contract enforceability, upgrades and administrative keys
Permissioned versus public ledgers: control and accountability

modules.title: Prudential, Accounting and Balance Sheet Treatment
modules.summary: How participation affects capital, liquidity, accounting and balance sheet risk, including the treatment of crypto-asset exposures and the treasury implications of holding or issuing digital money.
objectives: Apply the Basel Committee prudential standard for crypto-asset exposures
Assess liquidity, concentration and counterparty risks of participation
Identify accounting and reporting questions before launch
syllabus: Basel Committee classification of tokenised assets and stablecoins
Liquidity risk, reserve investment and redemption pressure
Counterparty and concentration risk in issuers and platforms
Accounting recognition, disclosure and audit considerations

modules.title: Financial Crime, Operational Resilience and Cyber Risk
modules.summary: The financial crime, sanctions, operational and cyber risks that digital money and tokenisation introduce, and the controls the firm needs when transactions move onto shared or public ledgers.
objectives: Apply AML/CFT, sanctions and travel rule controls to digital money flows
Assess operational, cyber and third-party risks of ledger-based services
Design incident response and resilience arrangements for tokenised services
syllabus: FATF standards for stablecoins, unhosted wallets and the travel rule
Wallet screening, blockchain analytics and secondary market exposure
Key management, node operators and third-party dependency
Operational resilience and incident response for tokenised services

modules.title: Building the Firm's Participation Strategy
modules.summary: Brings the programme together into a structured decision on whether, where and how the firm should participate, with the governance, controls and supervisory engagement needed to proceed.
objectives: Evaluate strategic options from observer to issuer or infrastructure provider
Design governance, risk appetite and staged implementation for participation
Prepare to evidence readiness to supervisors before launch
syllabus: Strategic options: partner, distribute, hold, issue or operate
Business case, risk appetite and board approval
Pilots, sandboxes and engaging the authority early
Workshop: the firm's digital money and tokenisation roadmap

related.title: FinTech Business Models: Understanding and Supervising Innovation
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and firm compliance teams to understand how FinTech business models make money, grow and fail, and to assess their risks.

related.title: Quantum and Cryptographic Resilience for Firms
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping firms understand the quantum threat, build a cryptographic inventory, plan post-quantum migration and report readiness to the board and supervisors.

related.title: Crypto and Blockchain Fundamentals for Industry
related.summary: A ten-module foundation programme giving industry professionals and their advisers a practical understanding of blockchain, crypto-asset markets and service providers, and the risks and controls that matter.

related.title: Embedded Finance, Open Finance and Big Tech Partnerships
related.summary: A nine-module programme for firms building embedded finance, open finance and platform partnerships, covering partnership models, responsibility, partner oversight, data sharing, customer outcomes and exit.

related.title: Tokenisation of Financial Markets for Firms
related.summary: A ten-module programme for firms designing, launching and running tokenised securities, funds and platforms, from business case and legal structure to custody, settlement and supervisory engagement.

related.title: Agentic AI and Autonomous Finance for Firms
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping firms deploy AI agents that act and transact with sound authority, controls, governance and customer protection.
